clue.text: Assign new tasks to dyer, Pole, at work

indicators.note: things at work are busy and in motion, so the letters are set moving into a new order

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A manager gives a cloth-dyer and a Polish colleague fresh jobs on the factory floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To redeploy staff is to move them to different duties, which is giving them new tasks.

clue.text: Lecturer from Linacre, a dermatologist

indicators.note: taken from inside the following words, as a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the college name, the article and the start of the profession

explanation.surface: An academic at Linacre, an Oxford college, who happens to be a skin doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Linacre is an Oxford college; in British universities a Reader is a senior lecturer just below professor.
explanation.definitionFit: Reader is a British academic rank for a senior lecturer known for research.

clue.text: Slip into clubs, perhaps, in formal gear

blocks.note: a slip is a light dress or petticoat
clubs are one suit of playing cards; perhaps flags the example

explanation.surface: Changing into evening wear before heading to the nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' looks like nightspots but is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress suit is a man's formal evening outfit, such as tails, so it is formal clothing.

clue.text: Ban professional writer

blocks.note: short for professional
a scribe is a writer or copyist

explanation.surface: A call to censor a paid author.
explanation.definitionFit: To proscribe something is to forbid or outlaw it officially.

clue.text: How a week passes without planning ahead?

definitions.text: How a week passes without planning ahead?

blocks.note: literally, a week goes by in seven separate steps of twenty-four hours
the idiom for living in the present and not thinking about the future

explanation.walkthrough: The literal truth about a week doubles as the motto for taking life as it comes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for dealing with things as they arise rather than planning, and literally describes days passing singly.

clue.text: A model island, in the existing circumstances

blocks.note: taken as written
to model for an artist is to sit for them
IS is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A fashion model on an island, pictured just as things stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a noun but works as the verb: a model sits for a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning without change, in the present state of affairs.

clue.text: Impertinent, fool entering empty study

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so the first item sits within the other
an emptied word loses all its middle, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: just the first and last letters
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A cheeky idiot wanders into a deserted study.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassy describes someone cheeky and disrespectful, a synonym for being impertinent.

clue.text: Carried child, daughter, following onset of exhaustion

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the first item is placed behind the next one
onset is the beginning, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
first letter of the word
D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A parent lugged a little one and a daughter around until tiredness set in.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote is to carry or lug, so toted is its past tense meaning carried.

clue.text: Very clean, showing no sign of acne?

blocks.note: first meaning: immaculate, without a mark
second meaning, read literally: having no pimples on the skin

explanation.surface: A teenager's skin looks perfectly clear, without a single blemish.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful literal reading of the word as without spots.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means perfectly clean, and taken apart literally means free of pimples.

clue.text: Woodland plant's unusual name, distinct from all others

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so the word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the four letters rearranged
one as in unique, one of a kind

explanation.surface: A wild flower of the woods has a strange name that sets it apart from every other.
explanation.definitionFit: The wood anemone is a white-flowered spring plant common on woodland floors.

clue.text: Country hotels, new and old

indicators.note: making something new reshapes it, so these letters are put into a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, as fodder
O is the usual abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A travel note on a country whose hotels are a mix of modern and historic.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a mountain kingdom in southern Africa, entirely surrounded by South Africa.

clue.text: Tarzan in story old Greek translated

indicators.note: translating turns words into another form, so the letters are rendered in a new order

blocks.note: every letter of the three words is fodder

explanation.surface: Tarzan turns up in an ancient Greek tale rendered into English.
explanation.definitionFit: In Edgar Rice Burroughs' novels Tarzan is the heir to the title of Lord Greystoke, an English peer.

clue.text: Item of furniture in friendly professor's office

blocks.note: easy as in easy-going, relaxed and approachable
a professor holds a chair, the post of professorship

explanation.surface: Spotting a piece of furniture in the study of a genial academic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' means position here, not a room: a professorship is called a chair.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair is a large comfortable upholstered armchair, a piece of furniture.

clue.text: Sing version with new opening

indicators.note: a new opening means the first letter is swapped for a different one

blocks.note: a model of a car or phone is one version of it

explanation.surface: An instruction to perform a song in a fresh arrangement with a different intro.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not say which letter comes in; the definition and crossings supply it.
explanation.definitionFit: To yodel is to sing with rapid switches between chest voice and falsetto, as in Alpine song.

clue.text: Show good girls old harmonica

blocks.note: a musical is a stage show
G is the usual abbreviation for good
lasses are girls, chiefly in northern English and Scots usage

explanation.surface: A command to show off some nice girls an antique mouth organ.
explanation.walkthrough: The harmonica here is not the mouth organ but the glass harmonica, a set of tuned glasses played by rubbing the rims.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical glasses were the earlier name for the glass harmonica, an instrument of tuned glass bowls popular in the 18th century.

clue.text: Scaremongers unfortunately describing end of horror film

indicators.note: to describe can mean to trace around, so the first word goes around the others
the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is taken

blocks.note: alas expresses regret, much like unfortunately
the final letter
a film of moisture is a thin mist

explanation.surface: Panic-spreaders, sadly, giving away how a horror movie ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like a movie but is a thin haze; 'describing' is used in its geometric sense of drawing around.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarmists are people who spread needless fear, the same as scaremongers.

clue.text: Nickname: bore quits, upset

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the letters of both words are fodder

explanation.surface: A tedious person, given a mocking label, walks off in a huff.
explanation.definitionFit: A sobriquet is an informal or affectionate name for someone, another word for a nickname.

clue.text: Aristocrat - save one on steamship

blocks.note: save and bar both mean except, as in all bar one
taken as written
SS is the prefix for steamship; on places it after

explanation.surface: A noble passenger is rescued from a steamer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' looks like rescue but is the preposition meaning except.
explanation.definitionFit: A baroness holds the lowest rank of the British peerage, so she is a titled noble.

clue.text: According to the circumstances at sea, became shy, or otherwise

indicators.note: otherwise means in a different way, so the words are to be arranged differently

blocks.note: every letter of these four words is fodder

explanation.surface: A sailor turned bashful once out on the ocean, or maybe not, depending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' looks like an anagram signal itself, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom meaning depending on which situation actually applies.

clue.text: Admission made by expert touring about with small son

indicators.note: a tourist goes around a place, so one part is wrapped around the next

blocks.note: an ace is an expert
C is circa, Latin for about
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A specialist gets entry while travelling around with a young boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Access and admission both mean the right or means of entry to a place.

clue.text: Friend wearing very large gems

indicators.note: one wearing something has it around them, so the second part goes outside the first

blocks.note: OS is the clothing-size abbreviation for outsize
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A friend draped in enormous jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: OS (outsize) is a British label for extra-large clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Opals are iridescent precious stones, a kind of gem.

clue.text: Foreman blowing top in rage

indicators.note: losing one's top means the head is removed, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: a ganger is the foreman of a gang of labourers

explanation.surface: A site boss explodes with fury.
explanation.walkthrough: A ganger is a British word for the foreman of a work gang; 'blowing top' suggests losing your temper but removes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger is a strong feeling of displeasure, and rage is its extreme form.

clue.text: Rascal has most of large prawns

indicators.note: most of a word is all but a little of it, so its final letter is cut

blocks.note: scampi are large prawns, often served fried in breadcrumbs

explanation.surface: A rogue grabs the lion's share of the big prawns.
explanation.definitionFit: A scamp is a mischievous person, especially a child, much like a rascal.

clue.text: This person can't sleep - I can son, I'm drunk!

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters of these four words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A sleepless parent blurts out tipsily that they can, son, being drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: An insomniac is someone who habitually cannot get to sleep.

clue.text: Impress English party

blocks.note: ENG is the abbreviation for English
a rave is a big dance party

explanation.surface: A boast that a very English party will impress the guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impress' reads as dazzle but means to press a mark into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To engrave is to cut or stamp a design into a surface, the literal sense of impressing it.

clue.text: Old boy's remedy, not easily understood

blocks.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil, with the S of the possessive kept
a cure is a remedy

explanation.surface: A former schoolboy's home remedy that nobody can quite make sense of.
explanation.walkthrough: An old boy is a British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscure is unclear or hard to grasp, matching difficulty of understanding.

clue.text: Bark and fight close to doghouse

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

blocks.note: a scrap is a brawl or fight
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A dog barks and squabbles near its kennel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bark' looks like the dog's noise, but it is the verb meaning to graze the skin, as in barking a shin.
explanation.definitionFit: To bark your knee is to scrape the skin off it, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Wise having been involved with best places to visit online

indicators.note: being involved means mixed up together, so the letters are combined and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as fodder
taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: Wise surfers have learned which are the best spots on the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: Websites are collections of pages on the internet that users go to and browse.
